KnowGPO: Knowledge-Grouped Policy Optimization for Search Agents

Siqi Chen Affiliation: Zhejiang University Affiliation: Tencent.{siqichen,syl}@zju.edu.cn, daniellwang@tencent.com    Zhengxi Lu Affiliation: Zhejiang University    Yuchen Yan Affiliation: Zhejiang University    Xingyu Wu Affiliation: Zhejiang University Affiliation: Tencent.{siqichen,syl}@zju.edu.cn, daniellwang@tencent.com    Qipeng Chen Affiliation: Zhejiang University    Xin Zhang Affiliation: Tencent.{siqichen,syl}@zju.edu.cn, daniellwang@tencent.com    Aiting Liu Affiliation: Tencent.{siqichen,syl}@zju.edu.cn, daniellwang@tencent.com    Chao Deng Affiliation: Tencent.{siqichen,syl}@zju.edu.cn, daniellwang@tencent.com    Jie Liu Affiliation: Tencent.{siqichen,syl}@zju.edu.cn, daniellwang@tencent.com    Jin Ma Affiliation: Tencent.{siqichen,syl}@zju.edu.cn, daniellwang@tencent.com    Weiming Lu Affiliation: Zhejiang University    Jun Xiao Affiliation: Zhejiang University    Yongliang Shen ††thanks: Corresponding author Affiliation: Zhejiang University
Abstract

Deep search agents solve knowledge-intensive tasks through long-horizon, multi-turn interactions, where assigning credit to individual search decisions is fundamentally difficult. Outcome-based reinforcement learning provides only a single terminal reward shared across an entire trajectory. Recent process-supervision methods aim to assign credit at finer granularity, but they typically anchor credit to either surface-level trajectory states or model-internal signals, both of which become unreliable in deep search where observations are heterogeneous and retrieved contexts are long and noisy. We propose KnowGPO, a reinforcement learning framework that aligns trajectories by the task-relevant knowledge they have acquired rather than by their surface observations. For each query, KnowGPO decomposes the information required to derive the answer into atomic knowledge conditions, and represents the state of a trajectory at each step by the subset of conditions it has satisfied. Trajectories sharing the same knowledge state are grouped for within-group comparison, and the incremental knowledge gain between consecutive steps serves as an environment-grounded process reward. Experiments on Xbench, BrowseComp-ZH, and GAIA show KnowGPO consistently outperforms outcome-only (GRPO) and process-supervision baselines (GiGPO, IGPO) by 3.8 to 4.2 points, with our 8B model rivaling or exceeding most 32B open-source systems. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/KnowGPO.

1 Introduction

LLM-based deep search agents have become a powerful paradigm for knowledge-intensive problem solving, coordinating multi-turn search, evidence inspection, query reformulation, and termination decisions through language-model reasoning (Yao et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2026a). Unlike conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which typically follows a one-pass retrieve-then-read pipeline (Lewis et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024), deep search agents iteratively formulate queries, inspect evidence, update beliefs, and decide when to stop (Nakano et al., 2021; Li et al., 2025c). This makes deep search a long-horizon sequential decision problem, where success depends on adaptive decisions about what to search, what evidence to keep, and when to terminate. Because supervised fine-tuning mainly imitates surface behavior  (Nakano et al., 2021; Schick et al., 2023) and cannot optimize such strategic decisions, reinforcement learning has become central to training competitive deep search agents (Guo et al., 2025; Jin et al., 2025; Song et al., 2025).

However, applying reinforcement learning to deep search agents encounters three coupled difficulties in credit assignment (Figure 1). First, terminal outcome rewards used by group-relative methods such as GRPO (Shao et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2025; Song et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2025) are uniformly broadcast to every action, so a single final reward cannot reveal which intermediate decisions were useful, redundant, or harmful. Second, recent process-supervision methods such as GiGPO (Feng et al., 2025) that align trajectories by their intermediate states require state recurrence across trajectories, yet deep search rollouts seldom revisit the same observable state even when they acquire the same evidence. Third, dense process rewards derived from changes in the model’s predicted answer probability, as in IGPO (Wang et al., 2026), or from learned critics and rubric-based reward models (Shi et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b; Lu et al., 2026), provide denser signals but are driven by model-internal beliefs or learned proxies rather than by externally verified knowledge.

Deep search trajectories vary widely at the level of queries, pages, and reasoning traces, but converge on the same underlying quantity: the task-relevant knowledge they have accumulated toward the correct answer. This knowledge, not observations or model confidence, provides the natural signal for credit assignment in long-horizon search.

We propose Knowledge-Grouped Policy Optimization (KnowGPO), a RL framework that aligns trajectories by the task-relevant knowledge they have acquired rather than by their surface observations. For each query, we decompose the information required to derive the correct answer into a set of atomic knowledge conditions. At every step of a trajectory, we represent its state by the subset of conditions it has satisfied, called its knowledge state. We further define incremental knowledge gain, the increase in satisfied conditions between consecutive steps, as a process reward that scores each action’s immediate contribution. While knowledge-state grouping ensures only semantically comparable steps are contrasted, incremental gain provides the dense signal within each group, enabling fine-grained credit assignment without a learned critic. Trajectories sharing the same knowledge state are grouped for within-group comparison, yielding step-level advantages that combine with episode-level outcome advantages through a single mixing coefficient. The result is fine-grained credit assignment for long-horizon deep search without observation matching, without dependence on the model’s own confidence, and without a learned reward model.

We train Qwen3-8B with KnowGPO on three challenging deep search benchmarks: Xbench, BrowseComp-ZH, and GAIA. KnowGPO improves over outcome-only GRPO by 2.0% to 5.9% and consistently outperforms recent process-supervision baselines including GiGPO and IGPO, with the resulting 8B agent matching or surpassing open-source systems of up to 32B parameters.

In summary, our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We propose KnowGPO, a reinforcement learning framework that performs credit assignment in a query-specific knowledge state space rather than over surface observations, enabling within-group comparison across semantically equivalent trajectories.

  • •

    We introduce incremental knowledge gain as a process reward grounded in the environment, providing dense step-level supervision without observation matching, learned critics, or reliance on model-internal probabilities.

  • •

    We demonstrate that KnowGPO outperforms outcome-based and recent process-supervision baselines by 3.8% to 4.2% across three deep search benchmarks, with an 8B agent matching or surpassing open-source systems of up to 32B parameters.

2 Related Work

2.1 Reinforcement Learning for Search Agent

Reinforcement learning with verifiable outcome rewards has become the dominant paradigm for post-training deep search agents. Early systems train models to interleave search and reasoning through outcome-based optimization on multi-hop QA (Jin et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025), showing that group-relative methods such as GRPO scale to multi-turn tool use without learned value functions. Subsequent work scales this paradigm along two axes: harder data through knowledge graphs, web exploration, and synthetic multi-hop generation (Lu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a; Du et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2025; Chu et al., 2026; Team et al., 2026e; Team et al., 2026d), and refined reward shaping and policy gradient stability for long-horizon rollouts (Wu et al., 2026; Dong et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2025). Despite these advances, the supervisory signal in most systems remains a binary reward at the end of each trajectory, leaving the contribution of search decisions inside long rollouts unidentified.

2.2 Credit Assignment for Search Agents

A growing line of work aims to address long-horizon credit assignment through process-level supervision. GiGPO (Feng et al., 2025) extends GRPO with anchor-state grouping, computing step-level advantages by matching trajectories that revisit the same environment state; this mechanism requires reliable state recurrence, which is rare in deep search where retrieved contents and reasoning histories are open-ended. IGPO (Wang et al., 2026) instead derives dense step rewards from the model’s own probability of producing the correct answer, sidestepping state matching but anchoring the signal to internal confidence that can be biased by long, noisy retrieved contexts. A parallel direction introduces externally grounded supervision through learned reward models or rubric decompositions (Zhang et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2025), providing denser feedback than outcome rewards but relying on learned proxies whose calibration is itself a research question, and without producing step groupings that make semantically equivalent decisions directly comparable across trajectories. KnowGPO instead anchors credit assignment to an externally verifiable representation of progress, the set of satisfied atomic knowledge conditions, and uses this representation as both the grouping criterion for within-group comparison and the basis of a process reward grounded in the environment.

3 Method

3.1 Problem Formulation

We formulate deep search as a multi-turn sequential decision process. Given a query QQ and a reference answer y∗y^{*}, an agent interacts with a retrieval environment over time steps t∈{1,…,T}t\in\{1,\dots,T\}. At each step the agent produces a reasoning trace and an action at∈{search,answer}a_{t}\in\{\texttt{search},\texttt{answer}\} from its policy πθ(⋅∣ht,Q)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h_{t},Q), where ht=(a1,o1,…,at−1,ot−1)h_{t}=(a_{1},o_{1},\dots,a_{t-1},o_{t-1}) is the interaction history and oto_{t} is the observation returned by the environment (e.g., retrieved documents for search, or a terminal signal for answer). A complete trajectory is denoted τ=(a1,o1,…,aT,oT)\tau=(a_{1},o_{1},\dots,a_{T},o_{T}) and terminates with a binary outcome reward R⁡(τ)=𝕀⁡(ans​(τ)=y∗)R(\tau)=\mathbb{I}(\text{ans}(\tau)=y^{*}). We build on group-relative policy optimization, which estimates advantages from a group of NN trajectories sampled for the same QQ and avoids learning a separate value network. The challenge addressed throughout this section is that R⁡(τ)R(\tau) alone provides no signal for distinguishing useful, redundant, or harmful steps inside a long-horizon trajectory.

3.2 Knowledge State

A central design choice in KnowGPO is to abstract the progress of a search trajectory through the task-relevant knowledge it has acquired, rather than through its surface observations. We realize this abstraction in two steps: constructing a query-specific set of atomic knowledge conditions, and representing each trajectory step by the subset of conditions it has satisfied.

Knowledge conditions.

For each query QQ with reference answer y∗y^{*}, we construct a finite set of atomic knowledge conditions

𝒦⁡(Q)={k1,…,kK},\mathcal{K}(Q)=\{k_{1},\dots,k_{K}\}, (1)

where each kjk_{j} is a single-hop factual constraint needed to derive y∗y^{*}. Intuitively, 𝒦⁡(Q)\mathcal{K}(Q) encodes the answer’s logical skeleton: a trajectory cannot reliably produce y∗y^{*} without acquiring every kjk_{j}. We construct 𝒦⁡(Q)\mathcal{K}(Q) through a two-stage pipeline that first identifies the reasoning skeleton implied by QQ (with placeholders for unknown entities) and then grounds each placeholder using y∗y^{*} and a successful reference trajectory. This decoupling produces a trajectory-agnostic knowledge space and ensures three properties: each condition encodes a single fact (atomicity), the conditions jointly support the full reasoning chain to y∗y^{*} (completeness), and entity references remain consistent across the query, the answer, and the search trajectories (grounding consistency). Construction details and the prompts used at each stage are deferred to Appendix B.

Knowledge state.

Given 𝒦⁡(Q)\mathcal{K}(Q), we represent the state of a trajectory τi\tau_{i} at step tt by the subset of conditions it has satisfied so far. At each step, an LLM-based verifier inspects the new observation oi,to_{i,t} and outputs a binary vector Δ​𝐬i,t∈{0,1}K\Delta\mathbf{s}_{i,t}\in\{0,1\}^{K} indicating the set of conditions newly verifiable from oi,to_{i,t}:

[Δ​𝐬i,t]j=𝕀⁡(hi,t⊧kj).[\Delta\mathbf{s}_{i,t}]_{j}=\mathbb{I}\!\left(h_{i,t}\models k_{j}\right). (2)

We then monotonically accumulate these increments to obtain the cumulative knowledge state:

𝐬i,t=𝐬i,t−1∨Δ​𝐬i,t,𝐬i,0=𝟎K,\mathbf{s}_{i,t}=\mathbf{s}_{i,t-1}\vee\Delta\mathbf{s}_{i,t},\qquad\mathbf{s}_{i,0}=\mathbf{0}_{K}, (3)

where ∨\vee denotes element-wise OR. Monotonic accumulation reflects the fact that acquired knowledge cannot be unacquired, and absorbs transient verifier noise across nearby steps. The knowledge state 𝐬i,t\mathbf{s}_{i,t} defines a shared semantic space across episodes: two steps with the same 𝐬\mathbf{s} have, by construction, acquired the same set of task-relevant facts, regardless of which queries were issued, which pages were visited, or how reasoning was phrased in between. This is the property that surface observations fail to provide and that KnowGPO exploits in the next subsection.

3.3 Knowledge-Grouped Policy Optimization

Given the knowledge state representation, Know-GPO assigns credit at two levels. Episode-level advantages align the policy with the final task objective, and step-level advantages, computed by grouping steps under matched knowledge states, attribute credit to individual search decisions.

Episode-level advantage.

For each query QQ, we sample NN episodes {τi}i=1N\{\tau_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} from the current policy and compute the group-normalized advantage of episode ii as

AiE=R⁡(τi)−μσ+ε,A_{i}^{E}=\frac{R(\tau_{i})-\mu}{\sigma+\varepsilon}, (4)

where μ\mu and σ\sigma are the empirical mean and standard deviation of {R⁡(τi)}i=1N\{R(\tau_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}, and ε\varepsilon is a small constant for numerical stability. This is the standard outcome-based group advantage of GRPO.

Step-level advantage via knowledge-grouped comparison.

To attribute credit at the step-level, we exploit the fact that the knowledge state 𝐬~\tilde{\mathbf{s}} partitions the space of intermediate steps into semantically equivalent classes. Let 𝒰\mathcal{U} denote the set of distinct knowledge states observed across all NN episodes for query QQ. For each 𝐬~∈𝒰\tilde{\mathbf{s}}\in\mathcal{U}, we form a knowledge group

𝒢(𝐬~)={(i,t)|𝐬i,t=𝐬~,ai,t≠answer}\mathcal{G}(\tilde{\mathbf{s}})=\left\{(i,t)\;\middle|\;\mathbf{s}_{i,t}=\tilde{\mathbf{s}},\;a_{i,t}\neq\texttt{answer}\right\} (5)

containing every non-terminal step that starts from state 𝐬~\tilde{\mathbf{s}}. We then define the step-level reward as the incremental knowledge gain,

ri,t=‖𝐬i,t‖1−‖𝐬i,t−1‖1,r_{i,t}=\|\mathbf{s}_{i,t}\|_{1}-\|\mathbf{s}_{i,t-1}\|_{1}, (6)

which counts the number of new knowledge conditions satisfied by step (i,t)(i,t). The step-level advantage is the group-normalized incremental gain within 𝒢⁡(𝐬~)\mathcal{G}(\tilde{\mathbf{s}}):

Ai,tS=ri,t−μ𝐬~σ𝐬~+ε,A_{i,t}^{S}=\frac{r_{i,t}-\mu_{\tilde{\mathbf{s}}}}{\sigma_{\tilde{\mathbf{s}}}+\varepsilon}, (7)

where μ𝐬~\mu_{\tilde{\mathbf{s}}} and σ𝐬~\sigma_{\tilde{\mathbf{s}}} are computed over 𝒢⁡(𝐬~)\mathcal{G}(\tilde{\mathbf{s}}). Two features of this construction are important. First, all steps compared within a group share the same prior knowledge state, so Ai,tSA_{i,t}^{S} measures how much more (or less) a step contributes to knowledge acquisition than alternative actions taken from the same epistemic position. Second, the step-level signal is anchored to the environment through the verifier’s checks against 𝒦⁡(Q)\mathcal{K}(Q), rather than to surface observations or the policy’s own answer probabilities.

Combined objective.

For each step (i,t)(i,t), we combine the two advantages with a single mixing coefficient ω∈[0,1]\omega\in[0,1]:

Ai,t=(1−ω)​AiE+ω​Ai,tS.A_{i,t}=(1-\omega)\,A_{i}^{E}+\omega\,A_{i,t}^{S}. (8)

The episode-level term keeps optimization aligned with the final outcome and prevents the policy from collapsing onto local information-gathering behaviors. The step-level term provides dense, semantically grounded supervision that distinguishes between informative and redundant decisions sharing the same starting knowledge.

We optimize the policy with a PPO-style clipped objective (Schulman et al., 2017):

ℒKnowGPO​(θ)=\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{KnowGPO}}(\theta)= 𝔼[∑i,tmin(ρi,tAi,t,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{i,t}\min\!\Big(\rho_{i,t}\,A_{i,t},\right. (9)
clip(ρi,t, 1−ϵ, 1+ϵ)Ai,t)]\displaystyle\left.\quad\mathrm{clip}(\rho_{i,t},\,1-\epsilon,\,1+\epsilon)\,A_{i,t}\Big)\right]
−βDKL(πθ∥πref),\displaystyle-\;\beta\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\theta}\,\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\right),

The full procedure, including knowledge state verification and group construction, is summarized in Algorithm 1 (Appendix A).

4 Experiments

We evaluate KnowGPO on four research questions. First, does knowledge-grouped credit assignment yield consistent gains over outcome-only and process-supervision baselines (Section 4.2)? Second, are knowledge-state grouping and incremental knowledge gain each individually necessary (Section 4.3)? Third, does the knowledge state genuinely provide a better grouping anchor than surface observations (Section 4.4)? Fourth, how does KnowGPO change search behavior, and at what training cost (Section 4.5)?

4.1 Experimental Setup

Benchmarks.

We evaluate KnowGPO on three challenging deep search benchmarks that cover diverse question distributions and difficulty levels: Xbench (Xbench-Team, 2025) (covering the 2505 and 2510 splits), BrowseComp-ZH (Zhou et al., 2025), and the text-only subset of GAIA (Mialon et al., 2023). Following standard LLM-as-judge protocols, GPT-4o (OpenAI et al., 2024) judges whether the agent’s final response matches the ground truth. All evaluations follow each benchmark’s official protocol; we report the mean accuracy over 3 independent runs.

Baselines.

We compare KnowGPO against three representative reinforcement learning approaches, all trained from the same SFT checkpoint with identical data and tool environments. GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) uses only the binary outcome reward and is the dominant baseline in current open-source systems. GiGPO (Feng et al., 2025) introduces step-level credit assignment by grouping steps that revisit the same intermediate state and computing within-group advantages from discounted future returns. IGPO (Wang et al., 2026) assigns each step a dense reward equal to the increase in the model’s predicted probability of the correct answer. In addition, we report numbers from several state-of-the-art open-source and proprietary deep search agents for context; differences in training data, context length, and tool stacks limit direct comparison, and we mark such systems separately.

Implementation details.

All trained models use Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025) as the base model, with context extended to 128K tokens via YaRN (Peng et al., 2026). SFT is conducted with LlamaFactory (Zheng et al., 2024); RL training uses verl (Sheng et al., 2025). All baselines share the same SFT initialization, training data, learning rate, batch size, and rollout configuration as KnowGPO; only the advantage estimator and reward design differ. Knowledge state verification uses DeepSeek-v3.2 as the LLM verifier; the choice and its quality analysis are reported in Appendix C. Full hyperparameters are in Appendix E.

4.2 Main Results

Tables 1 and 2 report performance on all three benchmarks. We make two observations.

KnowGPO consistently outperforms both outcome-only and step-level baselines.

All RL approaches improve over SFT, confirming that explicit policy optimization is necessary for deep search agents. However, existing step-level methods show considerable cross-dataset variability: GiGPO degrades by 2.0% on Xbench-2505 relative to GRPO despite winning on BrowseComp-ZH, and IGPO matches GRPO on Xbench-2505 but barely improves on BrowseComp-ZH. KnowGPO is the only method that improves on every split, gaining 5.9% on BrowseComp-ZH and 5.2% on GAIA over GRPO, and exceeding the strongest step-level baseline by 1.5% and 2.3% on these two benchmarks. The averaged gain over the SFT initialization is 8.5%. We attribute this consistency to the fact that knowledge-grouped credit signals do not depend on either surface state recurrence or stable model confidence, both of which are particularly fragile on noisier benchmarks.

KnowGPO closes the gap to 32B open-sour-ce deep search agents at 8B scale.

On BrowseComp-ZH, KnowGPO reaches 38.8%, surpassing the same-scale WebExplorer-8B by 6.8% and the 32B WebSailor-32B and DeepDive-32B by 13.3% and 9.1% respectively, and trailing the strongest open-source system DeepMiner-32B-RL by only 1.3%. On Xbench-2505 it reaches 48.0%, outperforming the 8B MiroThinker-v1.0 by 12.6%. These results show that knowledge-grouped credit assignment narrows the gap to substantially larger open-source systems without proprietary data or larger backbones. A gap to proprietary systems remains, for example 23.5% to Kimi-K2.5 on BrowseComp-ZH and 28.1% to Claude-4-Sonnet on GAIA, which we attribute to training data scale, model capacity, and inference-time optimization beyond our scope.

Training dynamics across baselines.

Figure 3 tracks validation accuracy on Xbench-2505 in RL training. All four methods start from the same SFT checkpoint and follow comparable trajectories during the first 16 steps, after which they diverge. KnowGPO opens a clear gap by around step 20 and plateaus near step 32 at roughly 50%, while GRPO, GiGPO, and IGPO settle below 46%. The gap is consistent across the second half of training, suggesting that knowledge-grouped credit assignment provides a denser signal throughout rather than a small final-stage advantage.

4.3 Ablation Study

We next ablate the components of KnowGPO. The first ablation studies the mixing coefficient ω\omega; the second isolates the contributions of incremental knowledge gain and knowledge-state grouping; the third compares incremental gain against discounted future returns as a process reward. All ablations use the same SFT initialization and training setup as the main experiments.

The mixing coefficient ω\omega balances outcome and process supervision.

Table 3 sweeps ω∈{0,0.3,0.5}\omega\in\{0,0.3,0.5\}. Performance peaks at ω=0.3\omega=0.3 across all four splits. Setting ω=0\omega=0 disables step-level supervision yet still outperforms GRPO on BrowseComp-ZH and GAIA, suggesting that grouping by knowledge state implicitly regularizes learning even before any step reward is applied. Setting ω=0.5\omega=0.5 overweights process supervision and degrades on three of four splits, reflecting that excessive local optimization can pull the policy away from the terminal objective. We use ω=0.3\omega=0.3 throughout the rest of the paper.

Both incremental gain and knowledge-state grouping are individually necessary.

Table 4 decomposes KnowGPO against GRPO. Adding incremental knowledge gain to GRPO (+Δ\DeltaKG, applied without knowledge-state grouping) improves over GRPO by 1.0% to 2.8% across benchmarks, confirming that knowledge-grounded step rewards are useful even without proper grouping. Further introducing knowledge-state grouping (KnowGPO, full) yields an additional 1.0% to 4.2%, with the largest gain (+4.2%) on BrowseComp-ZH. The role of grouping is to restrict normalization to steps that share the same prior knowledge state, so that within-group comparison contrasts decisions made from the same epistemic position rather than across mixed positions; the ablation isolates this effect from the choice of process reward.

Incremental knowledge gain outperforms discounted future returns as a process reward.

Within the same knowledge-grouped framework, replacing incremental gain with the discounted future return GtG_{t} used by GiGPO drops accuracy by 3.0%, 6.0%, and 3.4% on Xbench-2505, BrowseComp-ZH, and GAIA respectively (Table 4, row "KnowGPO w/ GtG_{t}"). The two rewards differ in how much downstream stochasticity they absorb: GtG_{t} couples a step’s credit to all subsequent decisions and is sensitive to long-horizon noise, while incremental knowledge gain is a local, immediate signal that does not require waiting for the trajectory to end. The gap shows that, even when grouping is fixed, the choice of step reward materially matters for long-horizon credit assignment.

4.4 Why Knowledge-Based Grouping Works

The ablation shows that knowledge-state grouping matters in aggregate. We now examine why it works by directly measuring the grouping behavior of three candidate anchors on real rollouts.

Setup.

We sample 500 queries from Xbench and BrowseComp (Wei et al., 2025) and rollout the SFT checkpoint up to 16 times per query, producing 5,922 valid trajectories with 55,571 steps after filtering. We compare three grouping anchors: observation-anchored, matching steps by BGE-large cosine similarity over retrieved contents at threshold 0.9 (the protocol used by GiGPO); action-anchored, matching steps by similarity of generated queries; and knowledge-anchored (ours), matching steps by exact equality of accumulated knowledge state. Grouping quality is measured by the effective step ratio (ESR, fraction of steps in non-singleton groups), the singleton ratio, the mean non-singleton group size, and the cross-rollout coverage (average number of distinct rollouts per non-singleton group). Formal definitions are in Appendix D.

Knowledge state aligns far more steps than observation or action.

Table 5 reports the five metrics. Observation-based grouping, the anchor used by GiGPO, leaves only 51.8% of steps inside non-singleton groups and produces 79.4% singletons, which means most intended step-level comparisons cannot be executed: the within-group advantage degenerates to comparing a step with itself, providing no learning signal. Action-based grouping improves ESR to 79.4% but its singleton ratio is still 72.0%, indicating that even when two trajectories issue similar queries, the evidence they end up acquiring is rarely comparable. Knowledge-based grouping raises ESR to 97.8% and reduces singletons to 19.0%, while keeping cross-rollout coverage (4.66) close to the highest value across anchors. This last metric is important: it confirms that the gain is not an artifact of merging adjacent steps within the same rollout, but reflects alignment of semantically equivalent steps across independent trajectories. A qualitative case in Appendix D shows two steps with 0.987 retrieval similarity that are correctly separated by the knowledge anchor (one has acquired 0 of 12 conditions, the other 8 of 12), illustrating that surface similarity can hide drastic differences in actual search progress.

4.5 Search Behavior and Training Efficiency

KnowGPO learns to search adaptively, not just less.

Reducing redundant search is easy if the policy simply stops earlier on every query, but this would harm hard cases. To test for this failure mode, we partition 500 test queries by joint solving outcome and compare average search turns (Table 6). On queries solved exclusively by KnowGPO, KnowGPO uses 9.83 turns versus 11.55 for GRPO, a clear reduction in redundant exploration. On queries solved only by GRPO, KnowGPO still uses 10.36 turns, and on queries where both methods fail, it uses 10.85, the longest of all subsets. The agent does not uniformly shorten search; it shortens search when evidence becomes sufficient and continues searching when evidence remains scarce. A representative trajectory comparison in Appendix G shows GRPO overshooting a correct intermediate answer by four additional turns and overwriting it with a wrong one, a failure mode KnowGPO avoids.

Knowledge-grouped credit adds negligible training cost.

A natural concern with structured process supervision is overhead. We profile per-iteration time over three training epochs (Figure 4). The training budget is dominated by operations shared with GRPO: trajectory generation (2,574s), policy update (583s), and probability computation (310s). KnowGPO-specific operations are knowledge verification (356s), incremental gain computation (2.73s), and group construction (0.03s). Verification runs asynchronously and overlaps with the next rollout, so its wall-clock cost is hidden behind generation; the two pure-bookkeeping operations together account for less than 0.08% of the budget. Knowledge-grouped credit assignment is therefore essentially free compared to GRPO.

5 Conclusion

We presented KnowGPO, a reinforcement learning framework that assigns credit by aligning deep search trajectories through the task-relevant knowledge they have acquired, rather than through their surface observations. KnowGPO groups steps under matched knowledge states and uses incremental knowledge gain as a process reward grounded in the environment. Across Xbench, BrowseComp-ZH, and GAIA, KnowGPO improves over outcome-only and process-supervision baselines by 3.8% to 4.2%, with an 8B agent matching 32B open-source systems at training cost comparable to GRPO.

Limitations

KnowGPO assumes that progress in the target task can be characterized by a finite set of verifiable knowledge conditions, which fits knowledge-intensive search but not more open-ended agentic tasks whose progress is harder to discretize. The fidelity of the knowledge state also depends on an LLM verifier, and although we use a strong external model with monotonic accumulation to suppress transient noise, residual errors can still propagate into step-level advantages. Our construction pipeline additionally requires at least one successful reference trajectory per query to ground entity placeholders, which limits applicability to settings where successful rollouts are reachable at reasonable cost. Finally, all experiments use Qwen3-8B; whether the effects we observe transfer to substantially smaller or larger backbones, or to reasoning-trained initializations, remains to be verified.

Appendix A Algorithm Details

This appendix provides the full pseudocode of KnowGPO and the explicit training objective used for parameter updates. The procedure begins by sampling NN trajectories for each query and running the LLM verifier at every step to construct the knowledge state 𝐬i,t\mathbf{s}_{i,t}. Trajectories are then grouped by their preceding knowledge state, and step-level advantages are computed by within-group normalization of incremental knowledge gain. The episode-level outcome advantage and the step-level knowledge-grouped advantage are combined with a single mixing coefficient ω\omega and used as the per-token advantage in a PPO-style clipped objective.

Token-level advantage broadcast.

Within each step (i,t)(i,t), the advantage Ai,tA_{i,t} is broadcast uniformly across all tokens that compose the action ai,ta_{i,t} and its preceding reasoning trace, following standard practice in GRPO-style training. The clipping ratio ϵ\epsilon, KL coefficient β\beta, and reference policy πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} are inherited from the SFT checkpoint and are shared across all baselines we compare against.

Asynchronous verifier execution.

The verifier call on line 4 of Algorithm 1 is the heaviest operation introduced by KnowGPO. We run it asynchronously, in parallel with the next rollout batch, so that its wall-clock cost is hidden behind trajectory generation. Empirical timing in Section 4.5 confirms this overlap makes verification effectively free relative to GRPO.

Appendix B Knowledge Condition Construction

This appendix details the two-stage pipeline introduced in Section 3.2 for constructing the knowledge condition set 𝒦⁡(Q)\mathcal{K}(Q).

Three design principles.

We require 𝒦⁡(Q)\mathcal{K}(Q) to satisfy three properties. (i) Atomicity: each kjk_{j} encodes a single-hop factual constraint, avoiding compound multi-hop statements inside a single condition. (ii) Completeness: the set jointly supports the full reasoning chain from QQ to y∗y^{*}, so that omitting any kjk_{j} renders y∗y^{*} non-derivable. (iii) Grounding consistency: entities in each condition use consistent referential forms across QQ, y∗y^{*}, and search trajectories, so that hit determination is not destabilized by entity ambiguity.

Bipartite graph view.

We represent 𝒦⁡(Q)\mathcal{K}(Q) as a constraint-entity bipartite graph

G\displaystyle G =(VC∪VE,E),\displaystyle=(V_{C}\cup V_{E},E), (10)
VC\displaystyle V_{C} ={C1,…,Cm},\displaystyle=\{C_{1},\dots,C_{m}\},
VE\displaystyle V_{E} ={⟨E0⟩,⟨E1⟩,…},\displaystyle=\{\langle E_{0}\rangle,\langle E_{1}\rangle,\dots\},

where ⟨E0⟩\langle E_{0}\rangle is the target answer entity and an edge connects CiC_{i} to ⟨Ej⟩\langle E_{j}\rangle whenever CiC_{i} explicitly contains ⟨Ej⟩\langle E_{j}\rangle. We require GG to be connected under BFS from ⟨E0⟩\langle E_{0}\rangle, which ensures every entity in 𝒦⁡(Q)\mathcal{K}(Q) traces back to the answer through factual constraints and rules out isolated knowledge.

Two-stage construction.

Stage 1 (Query →\to Placeholder Knowledge). The first stage takes only QQ as input and outputs placeholder conditions that capture the reasoning skeleton implicit in the query. Entities are denoted by placeholders ⟨E0⟩,⟨E1⟩,…\langle E_{0}\rangle,\langle E_{1}\rangle,\dots, where ⟨E0⟩\langle E_{0}\rangle is fixed as the target answer entity. This stage is trajectory-agnostic and does not require access to y∗y^{*}.

Stage 2 (Placeholder Knowledge →\to Grounded Knowledge). The second stage takes QQ, y∗y^{*}, the Stage 1 placeholders, and a successful reference trajectory obtained via rejection sampling. The model grounds each placeholder ⟨Ej⟩\langle E_{j}\rangle to its real-world entity, producing the fully grounded 𝒦⁡(Q)\mathcal{K}(Q) used at training time.

Decoupling structural decomposition (Stage 1) from entity grounding (Stage 2) yields a trajectory-agnostic knowledge space whose structure does not depend on which particular rollout happens to succeed. The prompts used at each stage are shown below.

Appendix C Knowledge State Verifier

This appendix justifies our choice of LLM verifier and shows representative behavior. We compared five candidate verifiers on 200 held-out query-trajectory pairs with manually annotated ground truth: DeepSeek-v3.2 (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025), DeepSeek-v3.1 (DeepSeek, 2025a), DeepSeek-v3.1-Terminus (DeepSeek, 2025b), Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite (Comanici et al., 2025), and GPT-4o-mini. Each verifier inspects the cumulative interaction history and outputs, for every condition kj∈𝒦⁡(Q)k_{j}\in\mathcal{K}(Q), whether it is supported by the trajectory so far.

Selection metrics.

We report three metrics: Regression rate, the fraction of state updates that violate monotonicity (a knowledge condition flips from satisfied back to unsatisfied at a later step); Parse rate, the fraction of verifier outputs that successfully parse as valid JSON; and Agreement, the fraction of per-condition judgments that match human annotation. Table 7 shows DeepSeek-v3.2 leading on all three metrics, with 94.7% agreement and a 5.2% regression rate. We adopt it as the verifier throughout the paper.

Qualitative behavior.

The accuracy gap between verifiers is largely driven by how they handle multi-step evidence integration. DeepSeek-v3.2 synthesizes evidence across distant search steps, while weaker verifiers tend to focus narrowly on the most recent observation and miss earlier critical evidence. The following example illustrates this pattern.

Appendix D Grouping Quality: Extended Results

This appendix expands the analysis of Section 4.4. We formally define the four grouping-quality metrics used in Table 5 and present a representative case where observation-based and knowledge-based grouping disagree.

Setup recap.

We sample 500 queries from Xbench and BrowseComp, rollout the SFT checkpoint up to 16 times per query, and obtain 5,922 valid trajectories and 55,571 steps after filtering. Three anchors are compared: observation-anchored, using GiGPO’s original protocol (BGE-large cosine similarity over retrieved contents, threshold τ=0.9\tau=0.9); action-anchored, using the same similarity protocol over generated queries; and knowledge-anchored (ours), requiring exact equality of accumulated knowledge state.

Metric definitions.

Let 𝒢\mathcal{G} denote the set of all groups produced by an anchor. We report:

  • •

    Effective step ratio (ESR): the fraction of steps in non-singleton groups,

    ESR=∑g∈𝒢|g|⋅𝕀⁡(|g|≥2)∑g∈𝒢|g|.\mathrm{ESR}=\frac{\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}}|g|\cdot\mathbb{I}(|g|\geq 2)}{\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}}|g|}. (11)
  • •

    Singleton ratio (SR): the fraction of groups containing only one step,

    SR=|{g∈𝒢:|g|=1}||𝒢|.\mathrm{SR}=\frac{|\{g\in\mathcal{G}:|g|=1\}|}{|\mathcal{G}|}. (12)
  • •

    Mean non-singleton size (MeanNG): the average size of non-singleton groups,

    MeanNG=∑g∈𝒢,|g|≥2|g||{g∈𝒢:|g|≥2}|.\mathrm{MeanNG}=\frac{\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G},\,|g|\geq 2}|g|}{|\{g\in\mathcal{G}:|g|\geq 2\}|}. (13)
  • •

    Cross-rollout coverage (Cross): the average number of distinct rollouts contributing to each non-singleton group. This metric distinguishes genuine cross-trajectory alignment from local within-trajectory smoothing.

  • •

    ngroupsn_{\mathrm{groups}}: The size of the sample group associated with each grouping anchor.

Qualitative case.

The following example illustrates why surface similarity is unreliable. Trajectory 6 has acquired 0 of 12 knowledge conditions (still in exploration), while Trajectory 10 has acquired 8 of 12 (the target entity has been identified). Yet the retrieved-content embeddings of the two trajectories’ steps reach cosine similarity 0.987 because both happen to mention similar generic terms (Chinese fir, forest research, research laboratory). Observation-anchored grouping clusters the two steps together and ends up comparing an exploration step with a verification step. Knowledge-anchored grouping correctly separates them because their knowledge states differ.

Appendix E Implementation Details

This appendix provides the full implementation details of KnowGPO and its baselines, organized into three subsections: tool environment, training configuration, and prompt formats.

E.1 Tool Environment

The interactive environment exposes a single search action that routes queries to Xhub Search for Chinese queries or Google Search for English queries, with language detected via Unicode character ranges. The engine accepts batch inputs and returns the top-10 results per query, each comprising a title, URL, and snippet. To bound the context length consumed by retrieved evidence, snippets are compressed to an average of 300 tokens by a fine-tuned Qwen3-8B summarization model that preserves entities and key claims while removing boilerplate. Temporal sensitivity detection biases retrieval toward recent content for time-sensitive queries.

E.2 Training Configuration

Supervised fine-tuning.

We first SFT Qwen3-8B on a corpus of approximately 8,100 deep search trajectories, constructed by combining human demonstrations with model-assisted annotation. SFT runs on 8 A100 GPUs using LLaMAFactory with standard causal language modeling, for 3 epochs at learning rate 2×10−52\times 10^{-5} and effective batch size 64. The resulting checkpoint achieves over 98.5% format accuracy on ReAct-style tool invocations and is the shared initialization for all RL methods we compare.

Reinforcement learning.

Following SFT, we apply KnowGPO and the three RL baselines. Training data is selected from the same source distribution as SFT but filtered to the zone of proximal development, defined as queries with pass@5 ∈[0.4,0.6]\in[0.4,0.6] on the SFT checkpoint. This yields 649 high-quality training queries. RL runs on 64 NVIDIA H20 GPUs using verl at learning rate 1×10−61\times 10^{-6}, batch size 32 prompts with 16 rollouts each, KL penalty β=0.01\beta=0.01, for 3 training epochs. All RL methods share these settings; they differ only in the advantage estimator and reward design.

E.3 Prompt Formats

The system prompt defines the available tools and tool-calling format. The user prompt enforces language consistency and structured answer formatting.

Appendix F Referenced Deep Search Agents

The scores reported for external deep search agents in Tables 1 and 2 are taken from their official technical reports or earlier publications: MiniMax-M2.1 (MiniMax, 2026), DeepSeek-V3.1/V3.2/R1 (DeepSeek, 2025a; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025), GLM-4.5/4.7 (Team et al., 2025; GLM-5-Team et al., 2026), Kimi-K2.5 (Team et al., 2026a), Claude-4-Sonnet (Anthropic, 2025), OpenAI o3 (OpenAI, 2025b), WebExplorer-8B (Liu et al., 2025), WebSailor-7B/32B (Li et al., 2025b), ASearcher-Web-32B (Gao et al., 2025), DeepMiner-32B-RL (Du et al., 2026), DeepDive-9B/32B (Lu et al., 2025), and MiroThinker-v1.0/v1.5/v1.7 (Team et al., 2026d; Team et al., 2026c; Team et al., 2026b). We were unable to locate official references for GPT-5-High and Gemini-3.0-Pro at the time of writing and report numbers as released by their providers.

Appendix G Search Behavior: Case Study

This appendix expands the search-behavior analysis in Section 4.5 with the experimental setup of the search-turn statistics and a representative failure mode of GRPO that KnowGPO avoids.

Sampling.

We randomly sample 500 test instances spanning BrowseComp-ZH, Xbench-2505, Xbench-2510, and GAIA, and partition them by joint solving outcome between KnowGPO and GRPO: KnowGPO-only (127), GRPO-only (89), both pass (103), and both fail (181). Average search turns per subset are reported in Table 6.

Failure mode: over-search erases the answer.

The case below is typical of the GRPO-only failure region and illustrates a behavior KnowGPO avoids. The query asks for a specific word quoted in an academic article. Both methods recover the correct word by step 8. KnowGPO terminates because its knowledge state is saturated; GRPO continues for four more turns, retrieves paraphrastic snippets containing competing surface tokens (soften, satirize), and overwrites its earlier correct answer. The example shows that absent a stopping signal grounded in actual evidence, additional search can actively destroy a correct intermediate answer.
